question: A plain X-ray of the hands in a patient with long-standing inflammatory polyarthritis shows periarticular osteopenia, joint-space narrowing, and marginal erosions at the MCP joints without osteophytes. Which diagnosis do these radiographic features BEST support?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osteoarthritis produces subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation, joint-space narrowing (especially at DIP joints), and subchondral cysts — NOT periarticular osteopenia or marginal erosions.

Correct. The classic radiological triad of RA is: periarticular osteopenia (early), uniform joint-space narrowing (cartilage destruction), and marginal (bare-area) erosions at the MCP and PIP joints. Osteophytes are absent, distinguishing RA from OA.

Chronic tophaceous gout produces 'punched-out' para-articular erosions with overhanging edges and sclerotic margins (rat-bite erosions), typically at the first MTP joint — not periarticular osteopenia or diffuse MCP marginal erosions.

Psoriatic arthritis produces 'pencil-in-cup' erosions, bony proliferation (periostitis), and DIP joint involvement. Periarticular osteopenia is less prominent than in RA; osteoproliferation is a distinguishing feature.

overallFeedback.feedback: Periarticular osteopenia + marginal (bare-area) erosions at MCP joints WITHOUT osteophytes = rheumatoid arthritis. OA has osteophytes; gout has punched-out para-articular erosions; PsA has pencil-in-cup erosions and periostitis.

Excellent. The RA X-ray triad — periarticular osteopenia + joint-space narrowing + marginal erosions at MCPs/PIPs without osteophytes — is a high-yield distinction from OA (osteophytes), gout (punched-out erosions), and PsA (pencil-in-cup + periostitis).
